Little pocket mouse (Perognathus longimembris) is a small heteromyid rodent inhabiting arid and semi-arid regions of western North America, where it exhibits a suite of life-history traits finely tuned to resource-limited environments. Field studies conducted under controlled thermal conditions, specifically at a body temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], have documented that females give birth to an average of five pups per litter [N_R_i = five pups per litter], and typically produce approximately 1.25 litters each year [F_R_i = approximately 1.25 litters each year]. This reproductive output is relatively modest compared to larger muroid rodents, reflecting the constraints imposed by small body size and unpredictable food availability in desert habitats. Neonates emerge weighing just 0.9 grams [Wwb = 0.9 grams] at birth, a minute mass consistent with the altricial developmental mode characteristic of heteromyids. These altricial pups are entirely dependent on maternal care during the initial postnatal period, growing slowly as they transition from milk to solid foods.

The suckling juvenile stage in Perognathus longimembris is relatively protracted given the species' diminutive adult size, with pups reaching nutritional independence after a period that unfolds under the same thermal regime of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. Weaning occurs at 28 days since birth [tx = 28 days since birth], marking the point at which young animals cease suckling and begin foraging independently on seeds and other plant materials at a temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. At this developmental milestone, the wet weight at weaning averages 4 grams [Wwx = 4 grams], representing roughly half the mass of a fully grown adult. This gradual transition from milk dependence to self-feeding allows juveniles to develop the digestive and foraging skills necessary for survival in the harsh desert environment. The comparatively late weaning age, relative to other rodents of similar birth mass, may reflect the low nutritional quality of the maternal milk or the challenges associated with locating sufficient food resources in arid landscapes.

Gestation in Little pocket mouse requires 22 days [tg = 22 days] when measured at a body temperature of 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], a duration that is typical for heteromyid rodents of comparable body size. This relatively short gestation period stands in contrast to the extended developmental phases observed postnatally, suggesting a life-history strategy that minimizes the energetic burden on the gravid female during pregnancy while shifting substantial investment toward lactation and postnatal care. The interplay between gestation length and the subsequent suckling interval reveals a pattern common among desert-adapted small mammals, where rapid gestation allows females to allocate resources strategically according to the episodic availability of food. Embryogenesis proceeds quickly within the uterine environment, yet the resulting altricial neonates require extensive maternal attention before they can achieve independence.

Sexual maturation in females, based on data originally established for the closely related Ord's kangaroo rat (Dipodomys ordii) but applicable to Perognathus longimembris under similar thermal conditions, occurs at 151 days since birth [tp = 151 days since birth] at 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C]. This delayed attainment of puberty stands in marked contrast to the rapid gestation period, indicating that females invest considerable time in somatic growth and fat accumulation before initiating reproductive activity. Such a prolonged pre-reproductive phase is adaptive in unpredictable desert environments, where delaying breeding until a threshold body condition is achieved can significantly improve offspring survival. The age at first successful reproduction is therefore tightly linked to resource availability, with females in poorer-quality habitats potentially postponing their first litter beyond the typical 151-day milestone. This conservative reproductive strategy reduces the risk of reproductive failure during unfavorable conditions.

The maximum recorded longevity of Little pocket mouse in captivity reaches approximately 8.3 years [am = approximately 8.3 years] when individuals are maintained at 34.7 °C [T = 34.7 °C], an exceptionally long lifespan for such a small rodent. This extended survival, far exceeding that of many similarly sized murids, is often attributed to the species' low metabolic rate and its ability to enter torpor during periods of cold stress or food scarcity. At the upper end of the growth trajectory, adult individuals ultimately attain a wet weight of 8 grams [Wwi = 8 grams], representing the plateau body mass typical of fully grown, reproductively active animals in the wild. This ultimate size is generally reached within the first year of life, allowing young adults to achieve the physical condition necessary for successful reproduction. The combination of a small asymptotic mass, a prolonged lifespan, and a conservative reproductive schedule positions Perognathus longimembris as a classic example of a slow-paced life history in a highly variable and resource-limited environment.
